1184.title: Save the burning world
1184.hook: the world is burning; save it by whatever door it can be saved (Bilaval Var M3, ang 853)
1184.howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok of Guru Amar Das in kirtan and katha, and some recite its opening lines as a prayer for the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday: man too jot saroop hai. O mind, you are the form of light; know your origin. Your line was you are light.

A house is on fire. Smoke at the windows, people inside. Nobody on the lawn holds a meeting about which door is the proper one. Front door, back door, a ladder at the upstairs window: whichever opening gets someone out is the right one. Guru Amar Das, who spoke to the single mind, now pulls the camera all the way back. In a salok in the Var of Raga Bilaval, he looks at the whole world, sees it burning, and asks for it to be saved by any door at all.
screen: `A HOUSE ON FIRE.` → `WHICHEVER DOOR GETS THEM OUT.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD, BURNING.`

segments.voice: The salok, paraphrased: the world is burning; save it, Lord, by Your mercy. By whatever door it can be rescued, rescue it that way. It goes on: the True Guru shows the way of peace, through reflecting on the true Word, and Nanak knows no other who forgives. Three things to slow down for. First, who's being asked. This is a prayer to God, not a project plan for heroes. The rescuing is in the Lord's hands, and the Guru is the one asking. Second, what's burning. Some readers hear an inner fire: craving, anger, ego, a world on fire from the inside. Third, the phrase at the center: jit duarai, by whatever door. The salok doesn't name one entrance and close the others. It asks for mercy through whichever door will work. Sikhs read that phrase in more than one way. Some hear a wide generosity: the Guru wants everyone rescued and doesn't haggle over how. Others hear the Lord's freedom: God knows which door suits each person, and the asking leaves that choice to God. Some hold both. Either way, the prayer is open-handed. And it leaves a question for whoever says it: is there a door I could open myself? That's today's line.
screen: `A PRAYER, NOT A PLAN.` · `A FIRE FROM THE INSIDE.` · `JIT DUARAI: BY WHATEVER DOOR.` · `READ AS GENEROSITY, OR GOD'S FREEDOM.` · then, large: `BY ANY DOOR.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who seems to be burning a little right now, stressed, grieving or stuck, and instead of planning a rescue, ask which door is open to you: a message, a meal, a ride, a quiet stretch of listening. Let one door come clear, and rest there. If you pray, hold them in the salok's words: save them by whatever door they can be saved.
Save the burning world. Guru Amar Das's prayer in Raga Bilaval: the world is burning; by Your mercy, save it, by whatever door it can be saved. Today's word.
Your line: by any door. Even a small door, opened, counts for something. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1184 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO IS A TRUE SATI.`

1185.title: Who is a true sati
1185.hook: not those who burn on the husband's pyre, but those who live in faithfulness (Suhi Var M3, ang 787)
1185.howItsDone: Sikhs cite these saloks of Guru Amar Das from the Var of Raga Suhi in katha and in teaching about the Gurus' stand on the dignity of women and widows, and on the Gurus' rejection of widow burning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the burning world, and a prayer for it to be saved by whatever door it can be saved. Your line was by any door.

Some words carry a compliment and a wound at once. Sati is one. Around Guru Amar Das, it could name a faithful, virtuous woman. It could also name a widow who burned on her husband's funeral pyre, a practice found in parts of the society he lived in. A grieving woman could be pushed toward the fire by the very word that honored her. In the Var of Raga Suhi, Guru Amar Das takes that word and changes who it belongs to.
screen: `A COMPLIMENT AND A WOUND.` → `THE FUNERAL PYRE.` → `THE GURU TAKES THE WORD.`

segments.voice: His saloks, paraphrased. One says: they are not called satis who burn themselves with the bodies of the dead. Nanak, they are known as satis who die from the blow of separation. Another: they too are known as satis who live in modesty and contentment, who serve their Lord and rise each morning to remember Him. He doesn't throw the word away. He keeps it, and takes it off the pyre. Faithfulness stops being one terrible moment at a funeral and becomes a whole life: modesty, contentment, service, a morning remembered. And the love being measured isn't only love for a husband. In the language of the Granth, the soul can be the bride, and the Lord the Beloved. So the true sati is anyone, woman or man, whose heart aches at being apart from God and who lives faithfully because of it. Tradition remembers Guru Amar Das speaking against the burning of widows, and the Sikh Gurus honoring the dignity of women in their sangats. Today's text is part of that memory, in the Guru's own words: gentle in tone, firm in meaning. And notice who the salok has in view: a woman in grief. The Guru's answer is: live. Your faithfulness counts in a living life, not in ashes. If grief ever turns toward hurting yourself, please reach out now: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
screen: `NOT THOSE WHO BURN.` · `MODESTY, CONTENTMENT, SERVICE.` · `THE SOUL AS THE BRIDE.` · `LIVE: FAITHFULNESS IN A LIFE.` · then, large: `NOT THE PYRE.`

segments.voice: Hold in mind someone who has lost a husband, a wife or a partner, a grandmother, a neighbor, a friend's mom, and stay with them a while without pity. Notice what their life still holds, the way they keep going, the people they look after, the small faithful things they do, and let one simple gesture toward them come to mind: a call, a visit, a question about the person they lost. If you pray, hold them in Waheguru on each breath out.
Who is a true sati. Not the one who burns on the pyre, says Guru Amar Das, but the one who lives in modesty, contentment and service, and aches to be near the Lord. Today's word.

1186.title: Gurmukh and manmukh, deeper
1186.hook: he paints the one facing the Guru and the one facing only the self
1186.howItsDone: Gurmukh and manmukh run through Guru Amar Das's hymns, which Sikhs hear in kirtan and katha; in Sikh teaching, becoming gurmukh is a lifelong turning toward the Guru's Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the true sati: not the one who burns on the pyre, but the one who lives faithfully. Your line was not the pyre.

Which way is your face pointed right now? Not your body. Your attention. Toward the phone, the worry, the next thing you want? Toward someone you love? It's a small question, and Guru Amar Das builds a great deal on it. Near the start of this path we met two words: gurmukh, the one facing the Guru, and manmukh, the one facing only their own mind. In his hymns these aren't labels on a chart. He paints them, like two faces in the same crowded room.
screen: `WHICH WAY ARE YOU FACING?` → `TWO WORDS FROM THE START.` → `HE PAINTS THEM.`

segments.voice: Mukh means face. Gur-mukh, face toward the Guru. Man-mukh, face toward your own mind. Here are some of his strokes, paraphrased from his hymns in Sri Rag and elsewhere. The manmukh is called blind, not because they can't see, but because they see only themselves. They act in ego and call it achievement. They read and recite, yet don't understand. They wander, and the wandering feels like freedom. The gurmukh, in his hymns, is at ease. Speaks sweetly. Sees the One light in everyone. Isn't shaken by praise or blame. Lives in the world with the Name at the center. Now the deeper part. These aren't two kinds of people sorted at birth. They're two directions, and his hymns keep calling the manmukh to turn. The same person can face the Guru at breakfast and only themselves by lunch. That's why his language is so often about turning: the Word turns you around. In the Sikh view, you don't become a gurmukh by deciding you are one. You become one, again and again, by facing the Guru's teaching when the mind would rather face itself. Ego and the Name can't share one room, and which gets it depends on which way the face is turned. So the line today isn't a judgment on anyone. It's a direction.

segments.voice: Notice where your attention is facing right now, a worry, a want, a screen, without scolding yourself. Then turn it slowly toward the breath, toward someone you love, or toward a line of the Guru's Word you remember, like man too jot saroop hai, and when it drifts back, turn again: the turning is the practice. If you pray, let Waheguru mark each turn.
Gurmukh and manmukh. The one facing the Guru and the one facing only their own mind: in Guru Amar Das's hymns, two directions anyone can face. Today's word.
Your line: face the good. Turning again is always allowed. See you tomorrow.

1187.title: Dying in the Word
1187.hook: he speaks of dying to ego through the Word and living truly
1187.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the idea of dying in the Word in Guru Amar Das's hymns, sung in kirtan and explained in katha; it is lived through daily remembrance of the Name and seva done without seeking credit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmukh and manmukh: two directions of the face, not two kinds of people. Your line was face the good.

Some phrases sound alarming until you see them up close. An argument at the dinner table: someone is sure they're right, and your clever reply is loading. Then, for no reason anyone can see, you let it go. The reply dies unspoken. Something small in you has to lose for the evening to be saved. Guru Amar Das has a bold phrase for a much larger version of that moment: to die in the Word. It sounds like an ending. In his hymns it's the start of living.
screen: `THE CLEVER REPLY, LOADING.` → `SOMETHING SMALL HAS TO LOSE.` → `TO DIE IN THE WORD.`

segments.voice: In Sri Rag he says it like this, paraphrased: whoever dies in the Word stays dead, and does not die a second time. Through the Word the Lord is found, and love for the Name takes hold. So what dies? Not the body. Haumai, the ego, the I, I, mine. The Word, sabad, is the Guru's teaching; dying in it means letting that teaching put something other than me at the center, which ego never allows. Then the strange promise: you don't die a second time. Some readers take it this way: once ego's grip is broken in the Word, the fear of death and the round of coming and going lose their hold. Ten days ago, Guru Angad's salok gave this a picture: dying while alive. Sikhs call it jivat marna. It doesn't mean giving up on life, ever. It means living fully, with the self out of the driver's seat. If dark thoughts about your own life ever come, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number. Ego rarely dies in one heroic moment. It dies in dinner-table moments: the reply you don't fire, the credit you don't grab, the grudge you put down. Each is a small rehearsal of the big thing. And the verse is clear about where this leads. Not into gloom. What follows the dying is finding the Lord, and a love for the Name that takes hold.

1188.title: The manjis, deeper
1188.hook: his network of teachers, women and men, spread the sangat far
1188.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the manji system in histories of Guru Amar Das and in katha; today local gurdwaras and their sangats carry on the work of gathering people near home around the Guru's Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dying in the Word: ego's grip breaking, so that real living can start. Your line was die to ego.

A low wooden frame with rope woven across it, the household cot or seat of Punjabi courtyards. Nothing grand. Sit on it under a tree, and people can gather on the ground around you. Sikh tradition says that's the picture behind a word from Guru Amar Das's time: manji. He lived at Goindval, and the sangat kept growing in places far from his door. So, tradition says, he appointed teachers, women and men, to sit on a manji in their own region and hold the sangat together there.
screen: `A SMALL ROPE SEAT.` → `PEOPLE GATHER AROUND IT.` → `TEACHERS, WOMEN AND MEN.`

segments.voice: We've met the manjis before on this path, as a story. Today, look at the idea. First, a manji was a plain household seat, not a throne. The teacher sat close to the people, near enough to hear their questions. The authority came from the Guru's teaching, not from the furniture. Second, it moved the center outward. Instead of everyone traveling to one place, the sangat could meet near home. The Guru's Word, the langar's open row, the hymns: all of it could happen in a village courtyard. Third, tradition remembers women among these teachers; the Guru's network trusted them to lead. Accounts differ on the details. The heart of the telling is that the sangat spread far. And what was a manji meant to hold? Guru Nanak had already given the measure, in Sri Rag, paraphrased: how is the true sangat known? Where the One Name is spoken. That's the test. Not the size of the crowd, not the fame of the teacher, but whether the Name is spoken there. A Sikh who explains a hymn to a child, or invites a coworker to langar, does in a small way what the manjis did: carries the sangat a little further from the center, and sits close enough to listen.

If you pray, Waheguru can ride each breath out.

1189.title: The pilgrimages
1189.hook: tradition says he traveled with Sikhs to pilgrim sites and spoke against the pilgrim tax
1189.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Amar Das's journeys and the pilgrim tax in histories and katha, and they speak of an inward pilgrimage; gurdwaras are open to visitors without any fee.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manjis: plain seats where teachers, women and men, held the sangat near home. Your line was spread it far.

Pay here before you pray. A gate at the edge of a holy river, and someone collecting a fee from every traveler who wants to bathe. A family has walked for days. They're tired, they've saved for this, and now there's a charge just to reach the water. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Amar Das traveling with his Sikhs to pilgrim places, the crowded river towns where people came to bathe and remember God. And it remembers him speaking up about a tax laid on the pilgrims themselves.
screen: `PAY HERE BEFORE YOU PRAY.` → `A FAMILY AT THE RIVER GATE.` → `THE GURU AMONG THE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: Why would a Guru go to a pilgrim town at all? The Sikh Gurus taught that the true pilgrimage is inward. Guru Nanak puts it plainly in the Japji, paraphrased: I would bathe at the place of pilgrimage if that pleased Him; without pleasing Him, what good is the bathing? The Sikh word for a pilgrim place is tirath, and the Japji itself speaks of bathing at a tirath within. So Sikh tellings present it this way: he went where the people already were. Seekers gathered there, hungry for God, and the Guru met them in the crowd, sang the Word, and fed people. Not to mock their journey, but to share what the Gurus had found. Then the tax. Tradition says the Guru spoke against a charge laid on pilgrims, and some accounts say the emperor Akbar later lifted it. Whatever the details, the instinct runs through the stories of his time: no one should have to pay to come near God. Tradition says the well at Goindval was open to every caste. The langar row asks no fee. The Guru's Word is sung for anyone who walks in. A tax on pilgrims put a price on the very thing the Gurus kept giving away. So the line has two sides: free pilgrims from unfair charges, and remember that the pilgrimage inward needs no gate at all.

1190.title: Hymns of the mind
1190.hook: the mind is called restless, and the Word is its rest
1190.howItsDone: The Anand Sahib, with its verses to the restless mind, is part of the Sikh daily banis, and its opening and closing pauris are sung at the end of gatherings at the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrimages: the Guru among the pilgrims, and against a tax to come near God. Your line was free pilgrims.

It's the middle of the night, and a mind is trying to solve itself. It runs the plan again, the conversation again, the worst case again. Each time it gets a little cleverer, and a little less rested. Guru Amar Das, in the Anand, his song of bliss, turns to exactly that mind: e man chanchala, O restless mind. Not to scold it. To tell it something it keeps missing about cleverness, and about rest.
screen: `A MIND TRYING TO SOLVE ITSELF.` → `E MAN CHANCHALA.` → `WHAT CLEVERNESS MISSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, paraphrased: O restless mind, no one has found Him through cleverness. Listen, my mind, no one has found Him through cleverness. This enticing Maya has led people astray in doubt. And the verse ends where it began: O restless mind, no one has found Him through cleverness. Chanchal means restless, flickering, never still. The mind's favorite tool for getting still is cleverness: one more plan, one more argument, one more way of being sure. The Guru says that tool doesn't reach the place the mind is trying to get to. And he repeats the line, the way you'd say something twice to someone who's tired and not quite hearing you. So where is rest? The Anand's opening verse points the way, again paraphrased: I have found the True Guru, with ease, and my mind rings with rejoicing; sing the Word, all of you who have let it dwell in the mind. Rest, in that picture, comes through the Word. Not a new idea to win with, but the Guru's Word, heard, sung, remembered, until the mind stops having to hold itself up. You can't think your way into rest. But you can rest in the Word.
screen: `E MAN CHANCHALA: O RESTLESS MIND.` · `NOT FOUND THROUGH CLEVERNESS.` · `SAID AGAIN, FOR A TIRED LISTENER.` · `SING THE WORD, AT EASE.` · then, large: `REST IN THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Choose one line from these days, man too jot saroop hai, by any door, or simply Waheguru, and let it ride the breath, in and out. When the mind starts solving, planning or arguing, don't fight it with more cleverness; just lay it back down on the line, the way you'd lay a tired child back on a pillow. The line holds the mind.
